chunks: CMOS power and efficiency analysis. The question: CMOS efficiency analysis. How does operational frequency impact efficiency? What about logic/swing levels? Rise/fall times?
CMOS wastes very little power because it only takes energy when it switches.
Each time an output charges and discharges its load, it burns a fixed amount of energy that depends on the load and the supply voltage.
Average power is that energy times how often it happens.
Think of filling and emptying a bucket. Filling it costs a bucket's worth of energy from the supply. Emptying it throws that away.
The bigger the bucket, the higher the water level, and the more often you do it, the more you spend. The level matters most, because the cost goes up with its square.
Dynamic power is quadratic in supply voltage. Dropping from 3. 3 volts to 1. 8 volts cuts it by (1. 8 over 3. 3) squared equals 0. 30 .
A reduced swing from a high supply (dashed) only saves linearly, so the low swing should come from a low supply. Drag C or f: the curves scale in proportion, but the 0.
30 ratio between 3. 3 volts and 1. 8 volts never changes. Voltage is the only lever that acts quadratically.
Dynamic power: power burned while switching, P equals alpha C V DD squared f . Activity factor ( alpha ): the fraction of cycles that the node actually toggles.
Capacitance ( C ): how much charge the load soaks up per volt, like the width of the bucket. Measured in farads; 1 picofarads is a millionth of a millionth of a farad.
Frequency ( f ): how many cycles per second. 1 megahertz is a million per second. Leakage: a small current that flows even when idle.
Take a 10 picofarads load toggling every cycle ( alpha equals 1 ) at 1 megahertz from a 2 volts supply.
Power is 10 picofarads times 4 volts squared times 1 megahertz equals 40 µW.
Drop the supply to 1 volts and the power becomes 10 picofarads times 1 times 1 megahertz equals 10 µW, a quarter. Doubling the frequency would only double the power.
That is the whole idea.

"CMOS has no DC path in steady state, so power is mostly dynamic: every low-to-high transition draws CV DD squared from the supply, half stored on the load and half burned in the PMOS, and the discharge burns the stored half in the NMOS.
Average power is alpha CV DD to the 2f : linear in frequency, quadratic in supply and swing, independent of transistor resistance.
Rise and fall time only matter through short-circuit current, which grows with slow edges, plus there's leakage that doesn't depend on frequency.
Halving the supply cuts dynamic power by four."
